items.prompt: What is an atomic commit?
choices: One logical change, complete on its own
A commit touching exactly one file
items.explanation: Atomic means one coherent logical change, regardless of size.

items.prompt: Which message hints at a bundled commit?
items.explanation: Vague umbrella wording usually signals unrelated changes lumped together.

items.prompt: What did git bisect return in the opening scenario?
choices: One commit that bundled a dozen changes
A list of all bad commits
items.explanation: Bisect returns a commit, not a line; the commit here was a bundle.

items.prompt: Can a large commit be atomic?
choices: No, atomic commits are always small
Yes, if it is one logical change
Only if it touches one file
items.explanation: Size does not decide it; coherence does.

items.prompt: Which is the better fix for the opening scenario?
choices: Write longer commit messages for the bundle
Commit one change at a time
items.explanation: The root cause was commit shape, so the fix is in how we commit.

items.prompt: A commit fixes a bug and also reformats an unrelated file. Atomic?
choices: Yes, if the message is long
items.explanation: Two separate ideas means two commits.

items.prompt: What does an atomic commit make equal?
choices: The number of files and the number of tests
The commit bisect finds and the change that broke things
items.explanation: When a commit is one change, finding it means finding the change.

items.prompt: Why do bundles feel efficient?
choices: One commit at the end of a session is less effort now
items.explanation: The cost is pushed onto every later reader.

items.prompt: A commit adds a new `formatPrice` helper and uses it in 12 files. Is it atomic?
choices: No: it touches more than a few files
No: helpers and call sites must be separate commits
Yes: one change (introduce the helper and adopt it), even across many files
Only if it changes fewer than 100 lines
items.explanation: Atomicity is about one coherent idea. Helper plus adoption is one idea; file count is irrelevant.
items.reference:
Atomic commit
1️⃣ One logical change
✅ Complete and coherent on its own
🚫 Not a rule about size or file count
Why: bisect, review, and revert can each point at exactly one idea.
items.learnMore:
Coherence, not size

An atomic commit holds one logical change. A rename across 40 files can be atomic; a 3-line commit mixing a fix and a reformat is not.

Common mistake

Equating atomic with tiny. The test is whether the commit is one idea.
items.reflection: Think of a recipe card edited by several cooks. What would make one cook's edit easy to accept or undo on its own?

items.prompt: Which commit is NOT atomic?
choices: test: add cases for the empty cart
fix: handle empty cart total, plus re-indent of the whole file
items.explanation: The re-indent is a second, unrelated change riding along with the fix.

Run bisect again to go deeper into the commit

items.explanation: Bisect has no resolution below the commit; re-running it cannot go deeper, and reverting loses the good changes.

items.prompt: How does bisect search?
choices: It tests every commit from oldest to newest
It repeatedly tests the midpoint and discards half
It reads commit messages for keywords
items.explanation: That is binary search.

items.prompt: Roughly how many tests for 16 commits?
What does bisect ask at each step?
choices: Is this commit good or bad?
items.explanation: The midpoint answer decides which half survives.

items.prompt: History doubles. How many extra tests?
items.explanation: Each doubling needs exactly one more halving.

items.prompt: What does bisect finally point at?
items.explanation: Its output is a commit.

items.prompt: What does bisect need to start?
choices: A known good commit and a known bad one
items.explanation: Those two endpoints define the range.

items.prompt: Is bisect's search linear?
choices: Yes, one commit at a time
items.explanation: Halving gives logarithmic cost.

items.prompt: Roughly how many tests for 1000 commits?
items.explanation: log2(1000) is just under 10.

items.prompt: History grows from 64 to 256 commits. How many more tests does bisect need?
items.reference:
Halving the range
16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1
🧪 One test per halving
📈 Doubling history adds one test
Why: cost grows with log2 of the history, not with its length.
items.learnMore:
Binary search over history

Bisect assumes everything before the culprit is good and everything after is bad, so each test lets it discard half the commits.

Common mistake

Thinking bisect tests every commit in order.
items.reflection: You are looking for a page in a book where a typo first appears. How would you narrow it down, and how many page checks would a 1000-page book need?

items.prompt: A bug is reported but you only know it was fine six months ago. Why does bisect still work well?
choices: Bisect only examines commits from the last week
Bisect skips commits with long messages
Bisect uses the commit dates to guess the culprit
Cost grows with log2 of the commit count, so a big range adds only a few tests
items.explanation: Binary search makes a huge range cheap in tests.

items.prompt: Which type marks a bug fix?
items.explanation: fix is for corrections of faulty behavior.

items.prompt: Which type marks a new capability?
items.explanation: feat adds something users or callers can now do.

items.prompt: Which type fits only a README change?
items.explanation: docs is documentation only.

items.prompt: Which type fits adding tests with no production change?
items.explanation: test covers tests only.

items.prompt: Which type fits restructuring code with no behavior change?
items.explanation: That is the definition of refactor.

items.prompt: Which type fits bumping a dependency?
items.explanation: chore covers maintenance and tooling.

items.prompt: What is the format of a conventional commit?
items.explanation: The type comes first, then a colon.

items.prompt: What does a ! before the colon signal?
items.explanation: feat(api)!: ... flags a breaking change.

items.prompt: A change renames a function and also fixes the off-by-one inside it. What is the best approach?
choices: One refactor commit, since the rename came first
One fix commit, since fixes outrank refactors
Two commits: refactor for the rename, fix for the bug
items.explanation: Two intents, two types; each stays honest and revertable on its own.
items.reference:
Commit types
✨ feat: new capability
🐛 fix: bug fix
♻️ refactor: structure, same behavior
📝 docs / ✅ test / 🧹 chore
Why: the type is a promise about what the diff contains.
items.learnMore:
Types as a contract

A reader who sees refactor expects no behavior change. If behavior changes, the label misleads reviewers, release notes, and bisect users.

Common mistake

Using chore as a catch-all for anything awkward to classify.
items.reflection: Think of labelled boxes in a moving truck. What goes wrong when a box labelled 'books' also holds kitchen knives?

items.prompt: Which is the most misleading label?
choices: refactor: change rounding mode so totals differ by one cent
items.explanation: Changing observable behavior is not a refactor.

items.prompt: Why split formatting from logic changes?

items.prompt: What does git revert do?
choices: Deletes the old commit from history
Creates a new commit that undoes an earlier one
items.explanation: History stays intact; a new commit cancels the old one.

items.prompt: Who benefits from atomic commits during review?
choices: Reviewers judging one change at a time
items.explanation: Focused diffs are easier to evaluate.

items.prompt: Bundled commit contains a bug and good fixes. Reverting it...
items.explanation: Revert is all or nothing per commit.

items.prompt: After bisect finds an atomic commit, what is left?
choices: Nothing: the commit is the change
items.explanation: That is the payoff.

items.prompt: Which source feeds release notes?
items.explanation: Typed messages summarize without rereading diffs.

items.prompt: After bisect finds a bundled commit, what is left?
choices: Reading the diff to isolate the culprit
A second bisect inside the commit
items.explanation: Bisect cannot look inside a commit.

items.prompt: Which commit is easiest to roll back safely?
items.explanation: One idea, one clean undo.

items.prompt: Is atomicity only for bug hunting?
choices: No, it helps review, revert, and reading history
items.explanation: Anyone who later touches one change benefits.

items.prompt: A bad deploy came from one change inside a 14-file commit. Which statement is true?
choices: git revert can undo just the bad lines automatically
Bisect can split the commit for you
Reverting the commit would also undo its good changes
The good changes will be restored by CI
items.explanation: Revert is per commit, so bundles force a manual partial revert.
items.reference:
What atomicity buys
🔍 bisect: the commit is the change
👀 review: judge one change at a time
↩️ revert: undo only the bad part
Why: every later task starts from a clean unit of change.
items.learnMore:
Revert needs a clean unit

git revert undoes a whole commit. If the commit mixes a bad change with good ones, the good ones are undone too.

Common mistake

Assuming you can revert part of a commit with git revert alone.

items.prompt: Atomic history, 16 commits: how many bisect steps?
Bundled history of 9 commits: how many steps in the trace?
items.explanation: The trace tests c4, c6, c7 and lands on the mega-commit.

items.prompt: Where does bisect land in the bundled run?
items.explanation: It points at a commit, and the culprit is inside it.

items.prompt: Which run leaves manual work?
items.explanation: The mega-commit still hides 8 changes.

items.prompt: Is 3 steps better than 4 here?
choices: No, the answer is less actionable
items.explanation: Speed to a vague answer is not a win.

items.prompt: What did the atomic run end with?
choices: The exact change that caused the bug
items.explanation: c11 was the change.

items.prompt: What can bisect NOT do?
items.explanation: Commit is its resolution limit.

items.prompt: Which value was the bug introduced at in the atomic trace?
items.explanation: The final range collapsed to c11.

items.prompt: Compare: history A has 128 atomic commits; history B has 128 changes bundled into 16 commits of 8. Which statement is right?
choices: B is better because it needs fewer steps
A needs 7 steps and ends at one change; B needs 4 steps and ends at 8 changes
items.explanation: Fewer steps in B is bought by a coarser answer.
items.reference:
Steps vs. leftover work
✅ Atomic: 4 steps, 0 work left
📦 Bundled: 3 steps, 8 changes left to sort
⚖️ Fewer steps is not a better result
Why: step count measures search speed, not what the answer is worth.
items.learnMore:
Two different axes

Bisect narrowed 16 changes to one in 4 steps, or 16 changes to a mega-commit holding 8 in 3 steps. The second is faster but leaves a search behind.

Common mistake

Judging a bisect run only by how few tests it took.

items.prompt: Bisect checks out a commit that does not build. What do you do?
items.explanation: git bisect skip excludes it from the search.

items.prompt: Why not mark an unbuildable commit as bad?

items.explanation: A wrong answer misleads the search.

items.prompt: What makes a commit testable by bisect?
choices: It builds and the tests can run
items.explanation: Bisect needs a runnable snapshot.

items.prompt: Many skipped commits lead to...
choices: A range of suspects instead of one commit
items.explanation: Bisect cannot isolate a skipped commit.

items.prompt: Should each commit keep the project working?
items.explanation: Every snapshot may be tested.

items.prompt: Which splitting is risky?
choices: Adding a function in one commit and fixing its caller three commits later
items.explanation: Intermediate states break the build.

items.prompt: What command skips the current commit?
items.explanation: skip tells bisect it cannot judge the commit.

items.prompt: Is a broken-but-atomic commit fine?
choices: No, atomic also means coherent and complete
items.explanation: Coherence includes leaving things working.

items.prompt: Commits c5 to c8 do not compile, and the bug appears at c7. After skips, what can bisect report?
choices: Only that the first bad commit is one of c5 to c8
items.explanation: Skipped commits cannot be tested, so the answer is a range.
items.reference:
Bisect needs testable snapshots
🏗️ Each commit should build
⏭️ git bisect skip for broken ones
❓ Too many skips = range of suspects
Why: good or bad is only honest when the snapshot actually runs.

Atomic and working

Common mistake

items.prompt: A bug needs two commits to appear: a flag added in c8, read in c11. Where does bisect point?

Ask what you would write in the subject. If it needs 'and' between unrelated things, split. If the parts cannot work apart, keep them together.

Common mistake

Squashing a whole pull request and calling it atomic.
items.reflection: Think of chapters in a book. What makes a chapter break feel natural rather than arbitrary?
